I'm Ramesh. I share a hostel room with Jatin, so I only know what I saw and heard. In August he told his father he wanted to try the journalism elective before deciding whether to stay in law, like his father and grandfather. The calls changed after that. His father's voice came out of the phone loud enough for me to hear "ungrateful" twice. His mother only said, "You've got lost, beta."
Jatin stopped going home at weekends. He'd sit on his bed with two lists, one headed mine and one headed theirs, moving things between them. Once he asked me, "Do I even like arguing, or did I just grow up at that dinner table?" I didn't know what to say. He ate dinner alone a lot that month. I wish I'd sat with him more.

qa.a: He is trying to tell apart what he truly enjoys from what he simply absorbed growing up at his family's dinner table.

qa.a: Ramesh could have sat with him and asked what he had noticed so far, so Jatin felt less alone while sorting it out.

Sunday. After lunch Elizabeth, twenty, told her mother she wanted to stop going to the morning service for a while, just to think about what she herself believes. Her mother set down the plates. "After everything this family gave you? Ungrateful. You've lost your way." Elizabeth said sorry and went to her room, though she wasn't sure what for.
Wednesday. In the college library she drew two columns: what I still hold, and what I'm not sure of yet. Kindness to strangers, grace before meals and her grandmother's hymns went in the first. She sat alone until closing, too guilty to phone home and too unsure to talk to anyone.
Two weeks later. Anjali found her on the hostel steps. "You've been vanishing." Elizabeth showed her the columns. Anjali read them slowly and didn't argue. It was the first evening in weeks that Elizabeth didn't feel alone with the question.

qa.q: What two columns did Elizabeth draw in the library?
qa.a: What I still hold, and what I'm not sure of yet.

qa.a: She felt guilty for hurting her mother, even though she didn't believe asking honest questions was wrong.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Elizabeth's loneliness?
qa.a: Showing the columns to Anjali, who read them slowly without arguing, so she no longer carried the question alone.

qa.q: What might Elizabeth's mother be feeling when she calls her ungrateful?
qa.a: Her mother may feel hurt and afraid of losing something they share, even though it comes out as blame.

grounding: A young woman questioning her family's belief is called ungrateful and lost, feels guilt and loneliness, and tries to sort what she holds from what she inherited.

I'm Ritu, Kalyani's younger sister, so I've watched this from the sofa. For three years she did exactly what Papa planned: dental college, then the chair next to his in the family clinic. She never complained. She also stopped humming.
Last spring something shifted, though I can't say what went on inside her. She didn't quit or shout. She asked Papa if she could take Saturdays off to teach a children's dance class, just for three months, and she started taking all the clinic's child patients herself, because, she said, she likes making scared kids laugh.
At dinner she explained it carefully. "Papa, I'm keeping dentistry. I'm choosing the parts I love, and I want one day that's only mine." Papa was quiet, then passed her the dal. The humming came back.

qa.a: It suggests she feels lighter and more like herself now that part of her life is chosen by her.

qa.a: She kept dentistry, tested one small change with Saturdays, kept the child patients she loves, and explained it to Papa with respect.

Saturday. At his cousin's wedding an uncle asked Dhruv, twenty-five, about his plans. He heard himself recite them: an MBA next year, then take over the steel yard, like Papa. Every sentence was Papa's. Driving home he felt oddly hollow, and he didn't want to blame anyone for it.
Two weeks later. He didn't resign or apply abroad. He asked his father, Manoj, whether he could run the scrap-recycling pilot at the yard for six months, the one idea at work that kept him awake in a good way. He also joined a Sunday woodworking class, just to see.
A month later. Over breakfast he told Papa, "I'm staying in the business, but I want to choose my part of it. I'll decide about the MBA after the pilot." Manoj lowered his newspaper. "You've been thinking." "I have. You taught me to plan. I'm planning."

qa.q: What pilot did Dhruv ask to run at the yard?
qa.a: The scrap-recycling pilot, for six months.

qa.q: What did Dhruv feel driving home from the wedding, and why?
qa.a: He felt hollow because he realised every sentence of his plan was his father's, not his own.

qa.q: What made Dhruv's response wiser than resigning or simply carrying on?
qa.a: He tested small changes, the pilot and the woodworking class, before deciding, keeping the business he values while choosing his own part of it.

qa.q: How might Manoj feel hearing 'You taught me to plan. I'm planning'?
qa.a: He may feel respected rather than rejected, since Dhruv frames the change as using what his father taught him.

"Sonali, why is your tiffin still full?"
"Not hungry, Bhaiya."
Saurabh sat on the edge of her bed. "Something happened."
"Gunjan read my poem out in class. The one about Nani. I only showed it to her. Only her." Her voice cracked. "Everyone laughed at the line about Nani's hands."
"She's your best friend."
"Is. Was. I don't know." Sonali pushed her face into the pillow. "I told her everything, Bhaiya. Everything."
"Did she say sorry?"
"She said it was a joke." A long pause. "Maybe I shouldn't tell anyone anything ever."
Saurabh was quiet for a while. "Or maybe you tell things to someone who keeps them. It hurts because you trusted her. That part isn't your fault."

qa.a: Gunjan read out Sonali's poem about Nani.

qa.a: She is devastated because she had opened up fully to one best friend, and that trust was broken in front of the whole class.

qa.a: He suggests trusting people who keep secrets rather than closing off completely, and tells her the trust itself was not her fault.

qa.a: Gunjan may not have understood how private the poem was, or felt embarrassed and brushed it off, though that doesn't lessen Sonali's hurt.

I'm Francis, and I'm eleven now. When I was ten, Ankita was my best friend. We had a secret handshake and a den behind the water tank at the church hall. I told her my biggest secret: I still couldn't ride a bicycle without training wheels.
The next Monday the whole cycling group knew. Tony rang his bell at me all week. I felt like someone had pulled the floor away. I didn't eat lunch with Ankita for a month.
Later she said she only told one person. It still hurt. But I learned that telling a secret is like handing someone a glass. I still hand people glasses. I just watch first to see who holds them carefully.

qa.q: What secret did Francis tell Ankita?
qa.a: That Francis still couldn't ride a bicycle without training wheels.

qa.q: How did Francis feel when the cycling group found out?
qa.a: Francis felt like someone had pulled the floor away, let down by the one friend Francis trusted most. 😢

qa.q: What did Francis decide about sharing secrets after this?
qa.a: Francis still shares, but watches first to see who holds secrets carefully, instead of shutting everyone out.

qa.q: How might Ankita have felt when Francis stopped eating lunch with her?
qa.a: She might have felt guilty and lonely, perhaps not realising how much telling one person would hurt Francis.

grounding: A child looks back on sharing a biggest secret with one best friend, feeling devastated when she let it out, and learning to share more carefully rather than stop.

Everyone at the tuition centre near the Jorhat tea estate knew Bhupen, fifteen: the boy who did impressions of the sir, always had a joke and never seemed to study. On the bus home the back seat crowded around him.
He never mentioned that his mother had gone to work in Bengaluru in March, or that he cooked rice for his little brother every night and fell asleep over his books. When the others talked about their mothers' cooking, he cracked a joke and looked out of the window.
One evening the bus broke down and only Alka was left at the stand with him. "You're funny," she said, "but you always look tired." He almost laughed it off. Then he told her about the rice, and his mother's voice on the phone. Alka didn't say much. "My father works away too." They waited in silence, and it felt less lonely than the crowded back seat.

June. Chetan, twenty-six, came home from a party of forty people and sat on his bed feeling he had talked to no one. He scrolled through six hundred contacts and stopped at Leela, his college friend, whom he hadn't called in a year. He called. It was awkward. They agreed on every Wednesday.

Instead he went to the gallery on the last day, stood in front of her paintings and texted: "I messed up. I'm here now. Sorry." She came out with her arms folded, and then laughed. October. On a Wednesday call he told her what he'd told nobody: that he hated his job and felt stuck. She told him about her own panic before the opening. Afterwards the flat didn't feel so quiet.

qa.a: He forgot Leela's exhibition opening.

Bhupen Dada, her father's father, was up at dawn feeding the cow and humming, and every evening he sat on the stone wall naming the peaks for her as if introducing old friends. Abuela Jana had outlived a husband and a failed bakery, and she spent the meal asking the youngest cousins about their football. When they toasted her, she said, "I got plenty wrong, and I'd still do it all again."
Across the table, Abuela Carmen pushed her plate away. "Enjoy it while you're young, Priscila. It all turns to nothing." She had spent the morning listing what her children had failed to do for her.

Last week in the hostel I couldn't sleep, and I imagined being sixty: still in the bank job Baba found for me, the tabla gathering dust under the bed, never having told Baba I don't want his life. It frightened me so much that I've done nothing since. I've started the music school form eleven times and closed it, because every answer seemed not good enough.
Writing this, I can see how silly that is. If I'm scared of a wasted life, staying frozen is exactly how I'd waste it.
So I'm sending the form tonight, imperfect. And when I'm home in October I'll talk to Baba, with you there, if you'll sit with me.
Your brother,
Arnab

qa.q: How many times had Arnab started and closed the music school form?
qa.a: He had started it eleven times and closed it.

qa.q: What was Arnab afraid of when he imagined being sixty?
qa.a: He feared still being in the bank job Baba found, the tabla unused, never having told Baba he doesn't want that life.

qa.q: What realisation turned Arnab from frozen to acting?
qa.a: He saw that staying frozen was itself how he would waste his life, so he chose to send the form imperfect and talk to Baba.

qa.q: What might Kalyani Didi feel on reading this letter?
qa.a: She may feel trusted and protective, and glad he asked her to sit with him when he talks to Baba.

grounding: A student's fear of a wasted life at sixty first freezes him in perfectionism, then pushes him to act honestly now.
